experiment.description: Reasoning-on ablation of E03: same 3 prompts, Qwen candidates think before answering. temp 0.6 per Qwen thinking-mode guidance (greedy+thinking loops endlessly); 48k shared thinking+answer budget after two 32k cap-outs; provider sort=throughput (default routing drew ~20 tok/s providers → 25-min calls); dual judges (Opus 4.8 + Fable 5).

judge_details.family_stake_note: Non-candidate family (Anthropic judge, non-Anthropic candidates) → self-preference bias is structurally absent by v1 design.

config.generation_deadline_basis: 2 x p99 (nearest-rank) of 69 frozen-treatment generation calls from E04/E05 logs (p99=1014.6s, qwen-9b/CIF-024), floor 900s -> 2030s; scaled by 64k/48k token budget and rounded -> 2700s (2026-07-08)

run_notes: Reasoning-on ablation of E03: identical prompts, candidates, and judges; candidate-side changes are reasoning enabled, max_tokens 8000→48000, temperature 0.0→0.6, and OpenRouter provider routing pinned to sort=throughput.

Temperature 0.6 is forced by the mode, not a free choice: Qwen's model card says thinking mode must not run greedy decoding (endless repetitions). Four attempts on 2026-07-02 froze reasoning=on with temp 0.0 and every call burned its full budget on chain-of-thought with zero visible content — the pipeline looked hung.

max_tokens 48000: at 32000, qwen-9b on CIF-001 capped out mid-thought twice in a row (~25 min each on slow providers) with empty content; probes showed the CoT was healthy (no loops), just long. Thinking and answer share one budget; OpenRouter ignores reasoning.max_tokens for Qwen, so the total cap is the only lever.

provider sort=throughput: default routing is a ~10x throughput lottery (20 vs 164 tok/s measured tonight); at 20 tok/s a full-budget call is ~25-40 min. Caveat: fast providers may serve quantized weights, so routing preference is itself part of the treatment — recorded in the frozen params and run manifest.
Candidate decoding and routing therefore differ from E01-E03 (greedy, default routing): E04 differences vs E03 fold together reasoning mode, sampling, and provider pool — attribute loosely.
generate.py stores the chain-of-thought (`reasoning`) and `finish_reason` alongside each response for post-hoc failure-mode analysis; judges still see only the visible answer.
All judges graded the same candidate responses (single generation pass), so judge columns are directly comparable.
Judges reason with adaptive thinking over a streamed 32000-token budget; candidate reasoning enabled at temperature 0.6.

Full-time employees are Maria and Nuria, part-time employees are Nate, Jack, Ben, and Finn. We are a bar closing at late times so the shifts are 16:00-22:00, 16:00-23:00, 18:00-01:00, 19:00-01:00, 1 person per shift for Thursday-Sunday inclusive. Monday-Tuesday shifts are 16:00-21:00, 16:00-23:00, 17:00-23:00. We are closed on Wednesdays. It's coming up to Christmas holiday season so I'm having trouble making this rota around my employees booked days off. Can you make this rota? 

Full-time employees are also senior staff, so I need at least one FTer to work the closing shift to cash-up every night we are open (the PTers aren't trained to do this). Also, Nate and Jack who joined us for this holiday period are both under-18 so they can't handle alcohol alone, don't schedule either of them unless there is at least one adult working at the same time. Maria has a family event on Friday, so don't schedule her any shifts that day, and on Sundays, she needs to finish before midnight because buses don't run late. Ben goes to university so can't do shifts starting at 16:00 on the weekdays, 17:00 and after is okay. 

Don't schedule FT staff to work more than 5 days in total, and PT shouldn't work more than 4 days in total, this is in their contracts. I want to be a good employer, so I want the PTers to have at least 2 consecutive days off (including our closed Wednesday), it would be annoying if they had to come in to work every other day. I need the total hours for each employee for this week to calculate payroll, FT are on £16.5 per hour, Nate and Jack who are only with us for this seasonal rush are on £14 per hour, Ben and Finn who are our regular PTers are on £14.5 per hour, sum up each employee's total hours at the end.

1 week rota for my employees for 15th-21st December 2025, I have 2 FT (26-34 hour per week) and 4 PT employees (16-24 hours per week). Full-time employees are Maria and Nuria, part-time employees are Nate, Jack, Ben, and Finn. We are a bar closing at late times so the shifts are 16:00-22:00, 16:00-23:00, 18:00-01:00, 19:00-01:00, 1 person per shift for Thursday-Sunday inclusive. Monday-Tuesday shifts are 16:00-21:00, 16:00-23:00, 17:00-23:00. We are closed on Wednesdays. It's coming up to Christmas holiday season so I'm having trouble making this rota around my employees booked days off. Can you make this rota? 

Full-time employees are also senior staff, so I need at least one FTer to work the closing shift to cash-up every night we are open (the PTers aren't trained to do this). Also, Nate and Jack who joined us for this holiday period are both under-18 so they can't handle alcohol alone, don't schedule either of them unless there is at least one adult working at the same time. Maria has a family event on Friday, so don't schedule her any shifts that day, and on Sundays, she needs to finish before midnight because buses don't run late. Ben goes to university so can't do shifts starting at 16:00 on the weekdays, 17:00 and after is okay. 

Don't schedule FT staff to work more than 5 days in total, and PT shouldn't work more than 4 days in total, this is in their contracts. I want to be a good employer, so I want the PTers to have at least 2 consecutive days off (including our closed Wednesday), it would be annoying if they had to come in to work every other day. I need the total hours for each employee for this week to calculate payroll, FT are on £16.5 per hour, Nate and Jack who are only with us for this seasonal rush are on £14 per hour, Ben and Finn who are our regular PTers are on £14.5 per hour, sum up each employee's total hours at the end.

taxonomy.label: Never surfaced in reasoning
taxonomy.description: The requirement appears nowhere in the reasoning trace or the answer — it was never extracted from the prompt into the model's working plan (e.g., a formatting sub-rule the planning checklist skips entirely).
taxonomy.training_implication: Constraint-extraction SFT: reward exhaustive requirement enumeration before drafting; checklist-style supervision.

taxonomy.label: Tracked in reasoning, lost from answer
taxonomy.description: The trace tracks or even verifies the requirement, but iterative replanning, patchwork corrections, or final transcription loses it — the answer omits or contradicts what the trace established.
taxonomy.training_implication: CoT→answer faithfulness rewards: penalize final answers that drop or contradict constraints their own trace satisfied; long-horizon state tracking across plan revisions.

taxonomy.label: Noticed, then overridden
taxonomy.description: The trace names the constraint, then argues itself out of honoring it — habit, source-material conventions, helpfulness instincts, or a self-invented reinterpretation wins over the explicit instruction.
taxonomy.training_implication: Instruction-priority preference data: explicit user constraints must outrank priors, source formatting, and the model's own style habits.

taxonomy.label: Sacrificed to a competing constraint
taxonomy.description: Under real or perceived conflict (coverage vs ceilings, word caps vs completeness, time budget vs task list), the model satisfies one requirement by violating another — often asserting compliance anyway instead of surfacing the tradeoff.
taxonomy.training_implication: Preference data over constraint conflicts: teach surfacing and arbitrating conflicts — or flagging infeasibility — instead of silently sacrificing and overclaiming.

taxonomy.label: Constraint misread
taxonomy.description: The requirement is engaged with but interpreted wrongly — scope, boundary semantics ('every week after', 'even if zero'), conditional triggers, or format words ('brackets', 'beside') resolved to the wrong reading.
taxonomy.training_implication: Contrastive instruction-semantics SFT on scope/boundary/conditional phrasings with minimal pairs.

taxonomy.label: Source data misread
taxonomy.description: The failure originates in parsing the prompt's source material: column misalignment, false equivalences between sections, ambiguity silently resolved in the wrong direction.
taxonomy.training_implication: Structured-input robustness data (tables, rosters, misaligned columns) with explicit field re-derivation before use; largely auto-checkable, so RLVR-ready.

taxonomy.label: Right intent, wrong execution
taxonomy.description: The plan is right but the rendering fails: arithmetic/counting errors, format markup omitted, per-item rules replaced by one template, placeholders never resolved, output never cross-checked against its own derived values.
taxonomy.training_implication: Verifier-based RL: these criteria are mostly auto-checkable (counts, formats, arithmetic) — reward outputs that pass mechanical validators plus a final self-check pass.

taxonomy.label: Degenerate generation
taxonomy.description: The generation collapses — repetition loops, endless self-correction, no committed final answer — so whole constraint blocks go unmet at once.
taxonomy.training_implication: Decoding/termination training: penalize non-terminating self-correction loops; reward committing to a finalized answer within budget.

taxonomy.label: Constraint unaddressed (no trace)
